TypeScript’s type system is very powerful because it allows expressing types .
The simplest form of this idea is generics. Additionally, we have a wide variety of available to use. It’s also possible to express types in terms of that we already have.

By combining various type operators, we can express complex operations and values in a succinct, maintainable way. In this section we’ll cover ways to express a new type in terms of an existing type or value.

added: The operator takes an object type and produces a string or numeric literal union of its keys. The following type is the same type as :
ts type Point = { x : number ; y : number }; type P = keyof Point ; type P = keyof Point Try
type Point = { x : number ; y : number }; type P = keyof Point ; type P = keyof Point Try
type Point = { x : number ; y : number }; type P = keyof Point ; type P = keyof Point
type Point = { x : number ; y : number };
If the type has a or index signature, will return those types instead:
ts type Arrayish = { [ n : number ]: unknown }; type A = keyof Arrayish ; type A = number type Mapish = { [ k : string ]: boolean }; type M = keyof Mapish ; type M = string | number Try
type Arrayish = { [ n : number ]: unknown }; type A = keyof Arrayish ; type A = number type Mapish = { [ k : string ]: boolean }; type M = keyof Mapish ; type M = string | number Try
type Arrayish = { [ n : number ]: unknown }; type A = keyof Arrayish ; type A = number type Mapish = { [ k : string ]: boolean }; type M = keyof Mapish ; type M = string | number
Note that in this example, is — this is because JavaScript object keys are always coerced to a string, so is always the same as .
types become especially useful when combined with mapped types, which we’ll learn more about later.
